items.summary: Recent video-based world models pair the scalability of autoregressive (AR) prediction with the visual quality of diffusion models. The choice of scene tokenizer is paramount for the optimal performance of each of these, both in terms of fidelity and semantics. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers yield exactly that: the first coarse tokens carry the clip's global semantics while later tokens further specify details. Existing flexible tokenizers only apply a representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, a target the decoder can partly meet from its noised input instead. We introduce SemanTok, a flexible video tokenizer that feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight heads that reconstruct them from each retained token prefix alone. SemanTok achieves high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size: a 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats a VideoFlexTok AR model $3.4\times$ its size, and larger SemanTok AR models further improve fidelity. It keeps semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and gives the decoder higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. It performs well in both reconstruction and generation, and its short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and give better generation fidelity, with pixel detail deferred to later tokens.
items.title: SemanTok: Predictable Semantic Tokens for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

items.summary: World models allow agents to plan in latent space by choosing a sequence of actions that most reduces the distance to a given goal state. Thus, planning can benefit from latent representations whose distances mirror commute-times in the environment. The spectral embedding space of the graph Laplacian provides such a representation, if it obeys a specific eigenvalue-dependent scaling. Unfortunately, instantiating the graph Laplacian is intractable in large, continuous environments. Self-supervised learning offers a natural route to such commute-time-preserving embeddings at scale. However, here we show that existing methods, which commonly encourage isotropic representations to prevent representational collapse, tend to degrade the "correct" eigenvalue-dependent scaling, leading to an inaccurate representation of commute times. To address this problem, we introduce Commute-Time-Preserving World Models (CTWMs), combining a latent displacement predictor and a log-determinant regularizer that prevents collapse, which provably recover the correctly scaled Laplacian representation under reversible deterministic dynamics and at the predictor's fixed point. In numerical simulations, CTWM matches or outperforms LeWM, a task-agnostic baseline, on several complex, continuous goal-reaching benchmarks, while using half the parameters.
items.title: Learning Commute-Time-Preserving World Models for Planning

items.summary: ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive environments whose rules and objectives must be inferred from observation. We present Kepler, an open-source harness that represents hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through retrospective transition checks and conditional prediction checks. Under one frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration, Kepler obtained a server-verified 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games, with no per-game model selection or score-conditioned reruns. On 181 of 183 completed levels, the final Opus attempt used no more actions than the corresponding median-human baseline. The retained board runs used 8,256 environment actions, of which 7,292 occurred in scored levels. Retained local provider-session records yield 858.0 million tokens, 97.37% cache reads, and a \$777.72 cost at September 1, 2026 API list-equivalent rates. We also report three evaluation failures: source-code leakage that produced an invalid perfect run, agents reconstructing a removed harness in a control condition, and autonomous repair masking a broken planner. A single-game observation case study showed that animation frames contained task-relevant information absent from settled text grids. Across the final Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol boards, 48 of 50 game-model cells reached 100. These results indicate that public-set score alone has limited discriminative value and motivate first-attempt, cost-conditioned, and verification-aware reporting.
items.title: Kepler: Auditable World Models for ARC-AGI-3

items.summary: Controlling an agent with vision requires being able to separate useful information from irrelevant background information. JEPA-style latent world models seem like a natural approach for this, as they do not perform pixel-level reconstruction; however, they are still sensitive to these distractor signals and experience latent collapse. In this work, we introduce Controllability Factorized JEPA (CF-JEPA), a JEPA-style world model which splits the latent space into controllable and uncontrollable subspaces. This factorization allows us to capture all the distractor information into the uncontrollable region, while we use the control-relevant latent information for our task. With this, we show comparable performance across 2D and 3D control tasks under nominal conditions and improved performance under distracted conditions, where CF-JEPA is the only model that does not experience latent collapse. We also validate our model under distracted conditions for a simulated robot task, highlighting the practical application of such a scheme.
items.title: CF-JEPA: Improving Robustness of JEPA World Models via Controllability Factorization

items.summary: A time series world model (TSWM) predicts a controlled system's state from its observed history and planned actions and exogenous inputs. Current approaches build forecasters with actions as covariates, trained and evaluated on prediction error under the executed plan. Yet world models compare unexecuted plans, but their responses to changed plans remain untested. We ask which design choices matter and whether accurate forecasters respond to changed plans as real systems do. We address both with a formalization and benchmark. The formalization separates state, actions and exogenous inputs, distinguishes continuous, mode and event actions, and introduces mechanism consistency, a metric built on declared action-state relations with known directions, such as a vasopressor raising blood pressure: it checks whether shifting an action moves the forecast in the declared direction. The benchmark consolidates eight public datasets with real actions from engineered infrastructure and clinical care, varying prediction space, plan fusion and plan encoding across seven backbones and five seeds. First, a frozen latent prediction space lowers MAE by 9.9% over observation space and gated output fusion lowers it by 12.7% over input concatenation on average, with both improving all eight datasets; temporal plan encoding changes average MAE by at most 2.2%. Second, prediction error and mechanism consistency diverge: the lowest-error configuration is at or below chance in consistency on four of five datasets with declared mechanisms, and no design choice avoids this. Finally, directional supervision, a loss penalizing the wrong-signed part of the response to a shifted action, significantly raises consistency on penalized mechanisms with no change in MAE. Together they give TSWMs a recipe: a frozen latent space and output-side fusion for accuracy, and a training objective for mechanism consistency.
items.title: On the Divergence of Accuracy and Mechanism Consistency in Time Series World Models

items.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) predict visual futures and robot actions, yet they remain susceptible to task-incomplete imagination, where plausible, action-consistent predictions omit the transition needed for task completion. In this paper, we show that this failure is not inherent to the world model backbone, but emerges when adapted for short-chunk control, which can repeatedly favor plausible local continuations over task-completing transitions. To address this, we introduce Completion Aware Guidance (CAG), a training-free sampling method that guides generation toward task completion. Across representative WAMs, CAG improves success from 64% to 70% on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and from 69% to 75% in zero-shot simulation, while reducing task-incomplete imagination from 79% to 40%.
items.title: Completion Aware Guidance for World Action Models

items.summary: 3D Gaussian avatars support fast rendering, however, their real-time animation is often challenged by the costly neural inference. We address this bottleneck and show that the animation of pretrained avatar models can be closely approximated by a linear combination of identity-independent blendshapes. Building on this finding, we introduce GALA (Gaussian Animation via Linear Approximation), a distillation method that replaces per-frame heavy neural decoding with a shallow coefficient predictor and a linear blend. To improve fidelity and reduce memory requirements, we propose to construct the basis using block-local PCA under a rendering-aware metric and a memory budget. Our method learns a shallow MLP network to predict blendshape coefficients and applies to various animation architectures without retraining original models. We validate GALA by accelerating the inference of three distinct avatar models for 3D animation of facial expressions and full-bodies with clothing dynamics. Across these models, our distillation generalizes to held-out identities and reduces CPU animation cost by up to three orders of magnitude while preserving most of the rendering quality. Excellent results of our method confirm the shared linear structure of learned avatar representations and enable highly efficient and accurate animation at frame rates reaching up to 60fps on mobile devices. Project page: https://ramazan793.github.io/gala/
items.title: One Basis to Animate Them All: Gaussian Blendshape Distillation for Real-Time Avatars

items.summary: Replication package for an empirical comparison of the retrieval engines an offline, memory-constrained on-device assistant can embed: SQLite/FTS5, DuckDB-FTS, in-memory BM25, an in-memory linear scan, MiniLM with HNSW on CPU, and the on-disk vector store sqlite-vec. Cost (latency, build time, footprint) and retrieval quality are measured together on WikiText-103, SQuAD, Project Gutenberg and the Turkish TQuAD set, with an embedded hybrid and a coverage-gated router, quantized and ONNX encoders, stronger small encoders, an isolated cost decomposition, a downstream answer-recall check, an incremental-update test, bootstrap confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests. The package holds all code, the result files, the published tables and figures, and two checking scripts: one re-derives every table value from the result files, the other redraws the figures and compares them with the published files. The SQuAD files and eleven public-domain Project Gutenberg works are included; the copyrighted Metamorphosis translation (Project Gutenberg eBook #5200) and TQuAD, whose repository has no license, are downloaded and checked against their SHA-256; the WikiText-103 scaling corpus is a separate file in this record. DATA_MANIFEST.txt lists the SHA-256 of every input. The lexical scaling measurement was repeated on one Android phone; everything else was measured on an x86 workstation, and energy was not measured. Code: MIT. Data: their own licenses (public domain for the eleven Gutenberg works, CC BY-SA 4.0 for SQuAD, CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL for WikiText-103).
tags: on-device retrieval; privacy-preserving search; embedded databases; SQLite FTS5; full-text indexing; vector search; retrieval-augmented generation; multilingual retrieval; Turkish; edge intelligence; reproducibility
items.title: On-Device, Privacy-Preserving Knowledge Retrieval for Context-Aware Assistants: A Multi-Engine Embedded-Retrieval Characterization on Real Multilingual Corpora (Replication Package)

items.summary: A persistent agent must decide both what to retain as information arrives and what to surface once a query appears, yet memory evaluations can confound these decisions by comparing methods that differ in both retention and selection. We build a streaming-recall benchmark crossing retention and selection rules and evaluate every condition on the same 300 seeded episodes. Holding access fixed, query-aware selection improves required-fact recall by 15.5 percentage points (95% CI: 12.8 to 18.2), whereas a mixed comparison that also changes history access reports a 68.7-point advantage, of which 53.2 points are attributable to access. Under bounded retention, query-aware, dense, and oracle selection reach the retention ceiling, and all 319 observed failures in the bounded recency condition are caused by eviction rather than ranking errors. Recall falls to 0% as targets recede sufficiently far into the past. Repeating the evaluation on SQuAD preserves the retention ceiling while showing that dense retrieval can outperform lexical retrieval on natural text. These results show that bounded-memory evaluations should hold access fixed and report retention and selection separately.
items.title: What Should an Agent Remember? Disentangling Retention from Retrieval in Bounded-Memory Evaluation

items.summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables, la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia, inferencia, confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias. El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única. Asimismo, incorpora procedimientos para auditoría me

The chain begins with the generalized relative entropy Lean verifies that equal-mass inputs reduce this functional to finite Kullback–Leibler divergence. The previously verified Chronos EN1–EN6 complete-coarse-graining Arrow increment and rate are then connected directly to this D_+ functional. An explicit calibration interface links the entropy Arrow to the older Chronos Change/Arrow/Action clock system without assuming that the two independently defined Arrow quantities are identical. The bridge is subsequently lifted from scalar expressions to diagonal matrices and traces. in the diagonal spectral representation. Similarity invariance is then formally established, removing dependence on the chosen basis. The final CEG6 stage instantiates the construction using Mathlib's finite Hermitian spectral theorem for an arbitrary positive-definite real matrix G. The canonical eigenvector unitary, its two-sided inverse, strictly positive eigenvalues, the operator-trace identity, and the scaled finite spectral Lambda relation are all kernel checked. All final stages, CEG0 v0.5, CEG1 v0.3, CEG2 v0.3, CEG3 v0.2, CEG4 v0.2, CEG5 v0.2, and CEG6 v0.1, passed static placeholder audits and Lean axiom audits. It does not assume that a Chronos physical state and an external geometric G-field are physically identical; where such a cross-framework state identification is required, the compatibility condition remains explicit in the formalization. The cumulative formal program connects the Chronos temporal framework to entropy production, generalized relative entropy, matrix and operator structure, positive-definite spectral geometry, gravity, and now an explicit experimentally testable prediction. CEG7 adds the next important step. It connects the previously verified Chronos radial time field and its Newtonian gravity correspondence to a proposed gradient-dependent effective gravitational coupling. items.summary: KV cache pruning reduces long-context inference memory usage by evicting less important key-value pairs. KVzip estimates importance through context reconstruction: prompting a model to repeat the context chunk by chunk. This achieves strong compression quality at the cost of additional forward passes. Learned approximations reduce this cost but require model-specific training. We analyze how KVzip identifies important cached information and show how to approximate its reconstruction scores using information already computed during prefill. These findings motivate EchoPress, a training-free method that approximates reconstruction attention using queries and keys from standard prefill. For each request, it reconstructs only the first chunk to calibrate importance scores for the remaining context. Experiments on LongBench and RULER with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that EchoPress matches KVzip in task accuracy across eviction ratios from 50% to 90%, while reducing compression overhead by a factor of 1.7-19.6 and total prefill time by a factor of up to 2.9. Code is available at https://github.com/ljwljwljwljw/kvpress/tree/echo-press.
items.title: EchoPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Pruning via Virtual Context Reconstruction

items.summary: Berggren's three matrices generate the tree of primitive Pythagorean triples and preserve the quadratic form x₁² + x₂² − x₃². Cha, Nguyen and Tauber (2018) built such trees for other integral ternary forms Q of signature (2,1). We ask whether the matrices alone determine Q. Main results: Recovery criterion (Theorem 3.1). A set of isometries of Q determines Q up to scale exactly when no nonzero vector is sent to plus or minus itself by all of them. Equivalently, the group they generate is not virtually abelian; for integral isometries, it acts irreducibly. The proof is elementary linear algebra and applies to arbitrary real groups. Berggren trees (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Remark 3.5). Any two generators determine Q in Berggren's tree and in each of the five trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber. The definition of a Berggren tree alone does not force this: the generators A and A² give a Berggren forest for x₁² + x₂² − x₃² whose two generators both yield edges but do not determine Q. Roots at a rational null line (Theorem 3.6). For a primitive null vector P with divisor G, the minimum of Q on (P^⊥ ∩ ℤ³) \ ℤP is S = |det(2J)|/(2G²). An explicit congruence, Gm ≡ −τ (mod S), decides which minimal vectors e + mP are roots. N-cusps (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Corollary 3.9). For Q = ax₁² + bx₁x₂ + cx₂² − Nx₃² with D = b² − 4ac < 0, all data at the null vectors (p, q, 1) are explicit. A minimal root exists there if and only if gcd(G, S) divides D/G, and in particular whenever D is cube-free. Recovery by integral reflections (Theorem 3.12, Proposition 3.13). Minimal roots at two or three distinct rational null lines yield three integral reflections that determine Q. The paper also relates the reflections in the trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber to minimal roots (Remark 3.17), and states an open question for trees produced by their construction.
items.title: The Inverse Berggren Tree Problem

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist [Data set]. Kaggle. https://doi.org/10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/195341 Official source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (`CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`).
items.title: Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB)

items.summary: Supplementary data and code accompanying the manuscript “An Evidence-Chain Provenance Framework for Tracing the Overseas Circulation of Oracle Bones: A GIS-Based Approach”. This package provides materials for editors and referees to check the study’s methods and results. It includes: (i) the Tier A–D evidence-classification coding scheme; (ii) circulation-pathway tables and CSV files aligned with Tables 1–3; (iii) record-level evidence codes underlying Fig. 6; (iv) an English evidence-ledger digest; (v) a bilingual Chinese–English concordance of cited Chinese-language sources and personal names; (vi) location notes for GIS visualizations; (vii) Python scripts used to generate Figs. 1–6; (viii) finished figure PNGs matching the manuscript; and (ix) a public-domain Natural Earth basemap for re-running Fig. 5. The study synthesizes published historical sources, museum catalogues, and publicly disclosed institutional records. No new laboratory, survey, or interview datasets were generated. Author-generated materials are shared under CC BY 4.0; copyrighted verbatim text of published sources is cited but not reproduced in full. Natural Earth data are public domain.
items.title: Supplementary for "An Evidence-Chain Provenance Framework for Tracing the Overseas Circulation of Oracle Bones: A GIS-Based Approach"

items.summary: This repository provides the compiled analysis inputs, R code, figure source data and GIS rasters supporting the manuscript “Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change”. Version 2.0 contains the final USA-intersection climatic-analogue reconstruction and its corresponding model predictions and spatial summaries. The historical introduction pool contains 18,562 species. The stage-transition models use 5,791 complete-case species, of which 4,088 species without a recorded invasion form the future candidate invasion-debt subset. Future predictions cover 12 combinations of two climate scenarios (SSP126 and SSP585), three periods (2041–2060, 2061–2080 and 2081–2100), and two global climate models (HadGEM3-GC31-LL and MPI-ESM1-2-HR). The archive contains: • Figure_data: XLSX source workbooks for main Figures 1–4, Supplementary Figures S1–S4 and Supplementary Tables S1–S15, together with the compiled species-level analysis dataset and current and future candidate-species predictions. • Code: R scripts, computational inputs and provenance documentation for the stage-transition models, climatic-analogue searches, future predictions, phylogenetic null analysis, temporal analyses, sensitivity analyses and publication source tables. • GIS_rasters: GeoTIFFs for the main and supplementary spatial figures. Main Figure 4 rasters contain sums within globally aligned 0.5° display cells; supplementary spatial rasters retain the native 10-arc-minute resolution. • Validation: execution records and numerical checks. • README files: instructions for reproducing the analyses, plotting the source data and interpreting the spatial fields. Current and future closest US climatic analogue cells are identified separately for each candidate species. POT is the sum of future predicted invasion probabilities assigned to future analogue cells. CHG is future grid-level transition potential minus current grid-level transition potential, with unassigned cells completed with zero. CHG therefore incorporates both changes in predicted probability and relocation of climatic analogues. POSDP is the sum of positive species-level changes assigned to future analogue cells; Supplementary Figure S3 reports its range across the two climate models. The analytical workflow was tested with R 4.3.3. Reproduction starts from the compiled historical master dataset, supplied phylogenetic inputs, prepared species climatic centroids and extracted WorldClim grid values. The package does not independently repeat every upstream archive-curation decision, manual stage-status assignment, GBIF download or occurrence-cleaning step. These boundaries and the optional XLSX and GeoTIFF export procedures are documented in the README. The historical count of 15,950 candidate invasion-debt species is retained for historical summaries; it is not the population used for future predictions. This release supersedes the earlier spatial outputs based on a rectangular climate-search domain. Future results should be interpreted as conditional model projections rather than evidence of a statistically established climate-driven increase in invasion. The repository record is distributed under CC BY 4.0. The software license included in Code/LICENSE and the original terms of third-party inputs remain applicable.
items.title: Data and code for "Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change"

items.summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.
items.title: Sunnycode v1 A Reproducible Framework for Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization in Urban LoRaWAN Networks

items.summary: Privacy-derived scientific materials for controlled studies of evidence access and adverse product content in AI assessment. The supplement contains synthetic materials, prompts, recorded model answers, terminal failures, assignment mappings, original stage-specific scoring and statistical implementations, reference results, and an offline CPU replay entrypoint. It includes the main local studies, the hosted-model study, historical screening, two common-interface qualification rounds, and the exploratory two-model pilot. Screening and development records are kept distinct from formal comparisons; reused answer aliases are not independent generations. The qualification amendment was made after qualification and before the exploratory pilot, and the subsequent proposed formal extension was not run. The findings do not establish a general advantage of pre-event defense, equivalence, or broad robustness. This is a redacted scientific derivative with a new integrity manifest: account authorizations, user dialogue, machine paths, hardware logs, original provider envelopes, encrypted reasoning, native token journals and model weights are excluded. CPU replay reproduces scores and statistics from the released scientific records; it does not regenerate answers or repeat the original private token/authorization/environment audits.
items.title: Scientific supplement for Evidence Access and Adverse Product Content in AI Assessment

items.summary: Tackling complex real-world tasks can exceed the capabilities of a single large language model (LLM), motivating the use of multi-agent workflows that coordinate specialized agents to work together on these tasks. Recent methods train LLMs to construct better workflows from execution outcomes, but they optimize only the workflow generator, while the other agents that build or execute each workflow remain fixed even though every outcome depends on all of them. However, extending training beyond the generator is challenging: the agents are coupled, and a workflow's outcome is a single sparse score that cannot tell which agent causes a failure. We propose FloWright, which leverages the workflow as a harness to optimize workflows. By introducing a hierarchical, structure-aware reward paradigm, FloWright enables one role to self-evolve and two or more roles to co-evolve, with no additional models, labels, or executions. Considering the limitation that workflows are commonly trained and evaluated on data that a single agent can already handle, we further propose DataWright, an adaptive data hardening approach that converts existing datasets into workflow-level tasks with increased difficulty. Across document, slide, chart, code, math, and finance tasks, small open models trained with FloWright achieve improved performance by up to $+7.41\%$, with co-evolving ($+5.03\%$) more roles gaining more than optimizing one of them alone ($+2.83\%$). Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/FloWright/.
items.title: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).
items.title: Extracting Reproducibility Metadata from Machine-Learning Papers: a Taxonomy of Silent Errors and the Cost of Human Verification

items.summary: Exploring the world of Bell inequalities requires numerical methods that scale effectively with the number of parties, inputs, and outputs. Such methods can be used to study large-scale Bell inequalities beyond the reach of analytic methods, to design experiments for violating more complicated Bell inequalities, and to enable applications of Bell inequality violation. Such applications include randomness generation and multi-agent coordination with restricted communication. However, current general purpose optimizers such as the see-saw method struggle to handle Bell inequalities with only a dozen inputs and outputs. We introduce an optimizer for the quantum value of a Bell inequality based on batched gradient descent (BGD). More precisely, our BGD optimizer is a differentiable search over feasible quantum strategies in which states and projective measurements are generated from unconstrained variables. The Bell expression is evaluated by a direct tensor contraction without forming the prohibitively large Bell operator. This formulation makes parallel random restarts inexpensive and is thus naturally implemented by a GPU. We evaluate our optimizer against the see-saw method and find a significant speedup for a wide variety of Bell inequality families. Implemented on a GPU, our BGD optimizer can optimize Bell inequalities in our numerical experiments with more than a thousand inputs or outputs within minutes. For these large-scale Bell inequalities, we also efficiently compute the classical value by enumerating possible strategies using a GPU or expressing the optimization as a mixed-integer linear program. Our optimizers can serve as numerical evaluation tools for Bell experiments and multi-agent coordination problems modeled by Bell inequalities with many inputs and outputs, a common feature of real-world scenarios such as high frequency trading and distributed systems.
items.title: Efficiently Optimizing the Quantum Value of Bell Inequalities using Batched Gradient Descent

items.summary: Code and text-free reproducibility artifacts for the manuscript “Saudi Arabic Automatic Speech Recognition and Dialect Identification Using Calibrated System Combination and Gated Multimodal Fusion,” currently under revision at Scientific Reports . The repository implements a Saudi Arabic automatic speech recognition framework using XLSR-53, XLS-R 300M, XLS-R 1B, and MMS-1B with validation-tuned KenLM decoding, evaluation under a dialect-normalized scoring convention applied to both references and hypotheses, and calibrated N-best system combination. The reproduced combined test WER is 32.49% , compared with 34.04% for the best single-model configuration. XLSR-53 was evaluated on a 1,652-utterance subset of the test set and is therefore treated as an indicative baseline. The repository also provides SaudiDID-X, a multimodal Saudi dialect identification framework using frozen multi-layer MMS-1B acoustic representations and frozen SaudiBERT text features with a residual adapter and gated fusion. The audio-only comparison is the acoustic branch of the same SaudiDID-X training run , not an independently trained model. The archived test macro-F1 values are 52.01% for the audio-only branch and 53.79% for SaudiDID-X. The release includes analysis and reference-training notebooks, configuration metadata, anonymized split identifiers, text-free per-utterance result artifacts, statistical-test outputs, figures, tables, checksums, and a verification script. Raw audio and third-party transcriptions are not redistributed because of source-specific licensing restrictions. v1.0.2: Documentation, provenance, and configuration-metadata corrections. Archived predictions, primary reported metrics, data splits, checksums, and computational implementation are unchanged. See CHANGELOG.md for the complete list of corrections. v1.0.1: Configuration-metadata corrections for the single-run reporting protocol and per-stage training hyperparameters. No result values changed.
items.title: SaudiArabic-ASR-DID: Multi-Model ASR and Multimodal Dialect Identification for Saudi Arabic

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package accompanying the manuscript “Cross-fire transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery after the 2021 wildfires in southwestern Türkiye”. The package contains the analysis-ready modelling sample, Google Earth Engine and Python analysis scripts, locked out-of-fold model predictions, model-selection records, sensitivity-analysis outputs, uncertainty and calibration results, derived tables and figures, random seeds, data dictionaries, provenance information, and supporting quality-control documentation. The study evaluates the transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery across five 2021 wildfire complexes in southwestern Türkiye using outer leave-one-fire-out validation and spatially blocked inner cross-validation. The repository supports reproduction and auditing of the reported analyses. Source Sentinel-2, CORINE Land Cover, EFFIS, MODIS MCD64A1, and other third-party datasets remain subject to their original providers’ terms and licences. Spectral recovery reported in this study should not be interpreted as complete biomass, ecosystem, or restoration recovery.
items.title: Reproducibility package for cross-fire transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery after the 2021 wildfires in southwestern Türkiye

items.summary: This archive accompanies “Provenance-Aware Quality Control for Heterogeneous Bioactivity Data” by Xin Gao. It contains cached benchmark and fresh-target prediction tables, finite-pair curation summaries, cross-repository comparison materials, figure source tables, frozen manifests, and reproduction code for the non-hosted analyses. Run `python3 tools/recalculate_public_limited_companion.py` after extraction. The standard-library checker reconstructs retained confusion counts, Matthews correlation coefficients, pairwise disagreement summaries, and repository disagreement tiers without network access. This is a cached-statistics reproduction, not an end-to-end replay of every raw data pipeline or a hosted-model rerun. The archive deliberately excludes hosted-model MAPK14 per-item and aggregate outputs, Figure 8 source material, and raw payload, CIF, and run files because accepted-account redistribution terms were not retrieved. This is a conservative packaging decision and does not claim that the excluded material is necessarily restricted. Software is MIT-licensed; ChEMBL-derived adaptations retain applicable CC BY-SA obligations. BindingDB source dumps and publisher PDFs are not included.
items.title: Public-limited companion materials for Provenance-Aware Quality Control for Heterogeneous Bioactivity Data

items.summary: This reproducibility archive accompanies the manuscript ‘PCMTL: Physics-Consistent and Uncertainty-Calibrated Multi-Task Learning for Trustworthy Multi-Property Polymer Screening’. It contains source code, frozen configurations, controlled software-verification fixtures and outputs, figures, manuscript and Supplementary files, environment specifications, licenses, and a provenance manifest for external production data. Production material-level claims require the external PolyOmics and PI1M resources listed in DATA_MANIFEST.csv and execution of python reproduce.py --config configs/main.yaml
items.title: PCMTL: Reproducibility Archive for Physics-Consistent, Uncertainty-Calibrated Polymer Screening.

items.summary: This record contains the replication package accompanying the article “DCMT-Cert: Empirical Adequacy Certification of Machine-Learning Data-Contract Gates.” The package provides the scripts, retained numerical outputs, analysis tables, audit materials, dataset manifests, source hashes, and checksum information required to reproduce and inspect the computational analyses reported in the article. The materials cover the paired clean-versus-clean harm calibration, the Stage 1 policy-development analysis, the Stage 2 confirmation analysis, all five prespecified operating profiles, policy selection and multiplicity analyses, baseline comparisons, broadened fault analyses, model-family validation, native Great Expectations validation, harm-threshold sensitivity, provenance and transfer audits, and supporting consistency checks. The package is organised using descriptive file names and is intended to permit independent inspection and reproduction of the reported computational results. The accompanying article defines the experimental protocol, scope of the empirical certificates, statistical interpretation, and limitations of the study.
items.title: Replication Package for "DCMT-Cert: Empirical Adequacy Certification of Machine-Learning Data-Contract Gates"

items.summary: World models allow agents to plan in latent space by choosing a sequence of actions that most reduces the distance to a given goal state. Thus, planning can benefit from latent representations whose distances mirror commute-times in the environment. The spectral embedding space of the graph Laplacian provides such a representation, if it obeys a specific eigenvalue-dependent scaling. Unfortunately, instantiating the graph Laplacian is intractable in large, continuous environments. Self-supervised learning offers a natural route to such commute-time-preserving embeddings at scale. However, here we show that existing methods, which commonly encourage isotropic representations to prevent representational collapse, tend to degrade the "correct" eigenvalue-dependent scaling, leading to an inaccurate representation of commute times. To address this problem, we introduce Commute-Time-Preserving World Models (CTWMs), combining a latent displacement predictor and a log-determinant regularizer that prevents collapse, which provably recover the correctly scaled Laplacian representation under reversible deterministic dynamics and at the predictor's fixed point. In numerical simulations, CTWM matches or outperforms LeWM, a task-agnostic baseline, on several complex, continuous goal-reaching benchmarks, while using half the parameters.
items.title: Learning Commute-Time-Preserving World Models for Planning

items.summary: Data and Python code accompanying the manuscript “Replication-Based Criteria Can Change the Selected Number of Clusters: A Seven-Criterion Audit of k-Means on Indonesian Provincial Environmental Data” (submitted to the Journal of Computing Theories and Applications). The package audits how the number of clusters, k, is selected for k-means on a small tabular dataset: the published components of Indonesia’s Environmental Quality Index (Indeks Kualitas Lingkungan Hidup) for 38 provinces, 2021–2024. Seven criteria are computed for k = 2 to 8: the within-cluster sum of squares (read visually and by two formal knee rules), silhouette width, the Davies–Bouldin and Calinski–Harabasz indices, the gap statistic, subsample stability (adjusted Rand index over 200 pairs of overlapping 80% subsamples) and agreement with Ward linkage. The scripts also run sensitivity analyses, a comparison of six clustering algorithms, fixed-centroid assignment across years, a leave-one-out comparison of regression models for the air quality component, permutation importance and exact Shapley values. Contents: data/ (index components 2021–2024; GRDP per capita and population density; a cell-level provenance audit), code/ (six analysis scripts and a plotting-style module), README.md (run order, variable dictionary and data sources), requirements.txt (pinned library versions), CITATION.cff and licence files. Running the six scripts in the order given in README.md reproduces every table and figure of the manuscript in about four minutes on a laptop (Python 3.11 or later). The indicator values are official statistics from Statistics Indonesia (Badan Pusat Statistik) and are reproduced unchanged. Please cite the original BPS tables as well as this record. Code: MIT licence. Data files: CC BY 4.0.
tags: k-means; number of clusters; cluster validation; clustering stability; adjusted Rand index; environmental quality index; Indonesia; reproducibility
items.title: Data and code for: Replication-Based Criteria Can Change the Selected Number of Clusters: A Seven-Criterion Audit of k-Means on Indonesian Provincial Environmental Data

The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.
items.title: Sunnycode v1 A Reproducible Framework for Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization in Urban LoRaWAN Networks

items.summary: Code and text-free reproducibility artifacts for the manuscript “Saudi Arabic Automatic Speech Recognition and Dialect Identification Using Calibrated System Combination and Gated Multimodal Fusion,” currently under revision at Scientific Reports . The repository implements a Saudi Arabic automatic speech recognition framework using XLSR-53, XLS-R 300M, XLS-R 1B, and MMS-1B with validation-tuned KenLM decoding, evaluation under a dialect-normalized scoring convention applied to both references and hypotheses, and calibrated N-best system combination. The reproduced combined test WER is 32.49% , compared with 34.04% for the best single-model configuration. XLSR-53 was evaluated on a 1,652-utterance subset of the test set and is therefore treated as an indicative baseline. The repository also provides SaudiDID-X, a multimodal Saudi dialect identification framework using frozen multi-layer MMS-1B acoustic representations and frozen SaudiBERT text features with a residual adapter and gated fusion. The audio-only comparison is the acoustic branch of the same SaudiDID-X training run , not an independently trained model. The archived test macro-F1 values are 52.01% for the audio-only branch and 53.79% for SaudiDID-X. The release includes analysis and reference-training notebooks, configuration metadata, anonymized split identifiers, text-free per-utterance result artifacts, statistical-test outputs, figures, tables, checksums, and a verification script. Raw audio and third-party transcriptions are not redistributed because of source-specific licensing restrictions. v1.0.2: Documentation, provenance, and configuration-metadata corrections. Archived predictions, primary reported metrics, data splits, checksums, and computational implementation are unchanged. See CHANGELOG.md for the complete list of corrections. v1.0.1: Configuration-metadata corrections for the single-run reporting protocol and per-stage training hyperparameters. No result values changed.
items.title: SaudiArabic-ASR-DID: Multi-Model ASR and Multimodal Dialect Identification for Saudi Arabic

items.summary: Privacy-derived scientific materials for controlled studies of evidence access and adverse product content in AI assessment. The supplement contains synthetic materials, prompts, recorded model answers, terminal failures, assignment mappings, original stage-specific scoring and statistical implementations, reference results, and an offline CPU replay entrypoint. It includes the main local studies, the hosted-model study, historical screening, two common-interface qualification rounds, and the exploratory two-model pilot. Screening and development records are kept distinct from formal comparisons; reused answer aliases are not independent generations. The qualification amendment was made after qualification and before the exploratory pilot, and the subsequent proposed formal extension was not run. The findings do not establish a general advantage of pre-event defense, equivalence, or broad robustness. This is a redacted scientific derivative with a new integrity manifest: account authorizations, user dialogue, machine paths, hardware logs, original provider envelopes, encrypted reasoning, native token journals and model weights are excluded. CPU replay reproduces scores and statistics from the released scientific records; it does not regenerate answers or repeat the original private token/authorization/environment audits.
items.title: Scientific supplement for Evidence Access and Adverse Product Content in AI Assessment
